claims.text: Deliberate addition of lightweight, high-melting-point elements promotes a fine-grained microstructure in lightweight HEAs.
Deliberate addition of lightweight elements induces high lattice distortion.
The fine-grained, distorted lattice impedes dislocation motion.
Lattice distortion impedes grain-boundary migration and thereby stabilizes the fine-grained microstructure.
The proposed lightweight HEA will retain a fine grain size during elevated-temperature exposure.
Lattice distortion lowers diffusion coefficients for oxygen and corrosive agents.
Persistent grain boundaries reduce effective diffusion lengths for corrosive species and slow oxidation kinetics.
Impeded dislocation movement and microstructural stabilization increase mechanical strength.
Restricted diffusion improves corrosion resistance.
Restricted diffusion improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Adding lightweight elements such as Al or Ti lowers alloy density relative to a baseline made from denser conventional elements.
The lightweight alloy is predicted to have higher yield strength than the identically processed baseline alloy.
The lightweight alloy is predicted to form a thinner or more protective oxide scale than the baseline alloy.
The lightweight alloy is predicted to have a lower corrosion rate than the baseline alloy.
The lightweight alloy is predicted to maintain a lower overall density than the conventional baseline HEA.
Both alloys will be synthesized, heat-treated, environmentally exposed, and mechanically tested under identical conditions as a controlled comparison.
At sufficiently high temperature, accelerated diffusion can cause grain coarsening or phase separation and eliminate the proposed benefits.
Lightweight-element concentrations above their solubility limits can produce deleterious precipitates and remove the strength and environmental-resistance improvements.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in yield strength, oxidation resistance, and corrosion resistance relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
Grain coarsening or deleterious phase formation during testing would falsify the proposed microstructural-stabilization hypothesis.
